description: Frog won't cross the pond on stepping stones of random sizes, so Fox builds a bridge he can trust: a fraction bar lies down and becomes a number line from 0 to 1. Frog's equal hops place 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 = 1, Robo learns to count hops (spaces) not ticks, thirds and sixths bridges place 2/3 and 5/6, and same-length lines show that 1/3 is bigger than 1/6.

youtube.title: Fractions on a Number Line! Unit Fractions for Kids | Grade 3 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Frog only likes hops that are all the same size, so Fox builds him a bridge: a fraction bar cut into fourths lies down and becomes a number line from 0 to 1. Count Frog's equal hops to place 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4, which is the same point as 1. Catch Robo's mistake (count the hops, not the tick marks), place 2/3 and 5/6 on thirds and sixths bridges, and compare fractions like 1/3 and 1/6 on lines of the same length.

What kids learn: a fraction is a number with its own spot on the number line; the bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts make 1 whole; the top number (numerator) tells how many hops; 4/4 = 1; more equal parts make smaller parts. For third graders (CCSS 3.NF.A.1, 3.NF.A.2, 3.NF.A.3).

Try at home: fold a paper strip in half and in half again to make fourths. Write 0 at one end, 1 at the other and 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 on the folds, then hop a toy along it. Use scissors with a grown-up, and at a real pond, look from the path with a grown-up.

do.text: Fractions on a Number Line
Frog wants to cross the pond to the picnic on the island.
I'll help! Stepping stones, coming right up!
Off you go, Frog! Hop, hop, hop!
tiny gap
huge gap!
Some frogs can jump more than twenty times their own body length. Why won't he go?
Frog only likes hops that are all the same size. Let me measure the gap.
Zero here at the bank, and the island is the end of one whole crossing.
Measured twice. Now let's build a bridge with equal hops. Let's build it and see!
First, the bridge. Zero is at our bank, and one is at the island.
The whole crossing is the distance from zero to one.
whole = 0 to 1
But Frog needs smaller hops than that. One giant hop is too far!
So here is my fraction bar. It is exactly as long as the bridge.
I cut it into four equal parts. That makes fourths.
Fourths! We cut shapes into fourths in grade two.
Here's a question. If the bar lies down, will the tick marks be equally spaced?
equal spaces?
Let's build it and see. The bar lies down on the bridge.
Each cut drops straight down and makes a tick mark.
Yes! The parts were equal, so the spaces are equal. Zero to one, cut into four equal spaces.
4 equal spaces
Fourths! Every space is the same size. Frog will love that.
Frog starts at zero. Each hop is one fourth of the whole.
One hop. One fourth.
Two hops. Two fourths.
Where will Frog land after three hops?
3 hops = ?
Three fourths! Three hops of one fourth.
One more hop, all the way to the island.
Four hops! Four fourths, and he's at one.
So four fourths and one are the same spot. Four fourths equals one whole.
Now look at the fraction three fourths.
The bottom number is four. Four equal parts make one whole.
denominator
The top number is three. That's how many hops Frog took.
numerator
Top number, numerator. Bottom number, denominator. Got it!
Long ago, people in ancient Egypt wrote most fractions as one part, like one third.
Your turn! Bottom number?
How many parts make one!
Top number?
How many hops!
Try it on your arm. Shoulder is zero, wrist is one. Four equal finger hops!

scenes.title: Count the hops, not the ticks

do.text: Wait. Let me count the marks myself.
One, two, three, four, five.
Five marks, so fifths!
Hmm. Fifths or fourths? What do you think?
fifths or fourths?
Count the hops, not the ticks. Hops are the spaces between marks.
Four spaces, four equal hops. So these are fourths.
The first mark is zero. That's where Frog starts. It isn't a hop.
Five marks make four spaces. I'll count hops from now on.
count the spaces
Let's build two more bridges, exactly the same length.
This one is cut into three equal parts. Thirds.
thirds: 3 equal spaces
And this one is cut into six equal parts. Sixths.
sixths: 6 equal spaces
Same zero, same one, same length. Only the number of equal parts changes.
Frog, show us two thirds.
Two hops of one third. Two thirds!
And three thirds lands on one, just like four fourths.
Now the sixths bridge. Where is five sixths?
Five hops of one sixth. Five sixths!
The bottom number tells how many equal parts. The top number counts the hops.
Hop along with us!
Zero to one, cut it fair!
Count the hops to get you there!
Equal spaces, every one!
Four hops of a fourth, and one is done!
Again!
Zero to one, cut it fair!
Count the hops to get you there!
Equal spaces, every one!
Four hops of a fourth, and one is done!
Bottom number?
How many parts make one!
denominator
Top number?
How many hops!
numerator
Here's an easy one. One sixth is bigger than one third.
Six is bigger than three, so one sixth must be bigger!
Hmm. Which is bigger, one third or one sixth? Think!
Let's put both on the bridges. One hop of a third.
And one hop of a sixth.
One third is farther from zero, so one third is bigger.
Cut the same whole into more equal parts, and each part gets smaller.
Oh! Six parts are smaller parts. So one sixth is smaller than one third.
Now two fourths and three fourths. Same size parts. Two hops first.
Then three hops.
Three hops go farther. So three fourths is bigger than two fourths!
One rule. We only compare fractions of the same whole, so our lines are the same length.
Zeros line up. Ones line up. A fair comparison!
Challenge time! Help us place the lily pads. Five tasks!
Task one. Where does a lily pad go for two thirds?
Two hops of one third. Right here!
Task two. Which is closer to one, five sixths or one sixth?
Five sixths! It's just one hop away from one.
Task three. This bridge is cut into eight equal parts. Where is three eighths?
The third hop. Three eighths!
Task four. Is three thirds the same point as one?
Yes! Three hops of a third reach one.
Task five. Which is bigger, one eighth or one fourth?
One fourth! Fewer equal parts make bigger parts.
Five for five! Great placing!
Quick quiz! A line from zero to one has six equal parts. What is the first mark after zero?
One sixth!
How many hops of one fourth get to one?
Four! Four fourths equals one.
Which is bigger, one half or one third?
One half. Two equal parts are bigger parts.
Which is bigger, two sixths or five sixths?
Five sixths. Five hops go farther than two.
Last one. I once said a line with five marks shows fifths. Fix it!
Five marks make four spaces, so it shows fourths. Count the hops!
5 marks = 4 spaces
Let's remember. A fraction is a number with its own spot on the line.
